## Definition

Use $\mathbb N$ for the natural-number index set (including zero) ([[def-natural-numbers]]), $\mathbb R$ for the real scalar field ([[def-real-numbers]]), and $\mathbb C$ with its real embedding and modulus ([[def-complex-numbers-and-arithmetic]], [[def-complex-conjugate-real-imaginary-part-and-modulus]]).

Let $N\ge2$, $h>0$, $k>0$, and $t_n=nk$. For the finite periodic grid put $J_N=\{0,\ldots,N-1\}$ and reduce every shifted index modulo $N$. A periodic grid function is a map $v:J_N\to\mathbb C$, with weighted norm
$$ \|v\|_{2,h}=\left(h\sum_{j=0}^{N-1}|v_j|^2\right)^{1/2}. $$
The infinite uniform grid has indices $j\in\mathbb Z$ and positions $x_j=jh$. On the periodic and infinite grids define
$$ (D_+v)_j=\frac{v_{j+1}-v_j}{h},\qquad (D_-v)_j=\frac{v_j-v_{j-1}}{h},\qquad (D_0v)_j=\frac{v_{j+1}-v_{j-1}}{2h},\qquad (\Delta_hv)_j=\frac{v_{j+1}-2v_j+v_{j-1}}{h^2}. $$
Use the inner product linear in its first entry,
$$ \langle p,q\rangle_{2,h}=h\sum_{j=0}^{N-1}p_j\overline{q_j},\qquad \langle D_+p,D_+q\rangle_{e,h}=h\sum_{j=0}^{N-1}(D_+p)_j\overline{(D_+q)_j}, $$
where the indices in $D_+$ are reduced periodically, and set $\|D_+p\|_{e,h}^2=\langle D_+p,D_+p\rangle_{e,h}$. The same definitions apply to real-valued grid functions.

For a finite interval of length $L=Nh$, use physical nodes $x_j=jh$ with indices $j=0,\ldots,N$. On its edges $j=0,\ldots,N-1$ define $(D_+v)_j=(v_{j+1}-v_j)/h$, and on interior nodes $j=1,\ldots,N-1$ use $(\Delta_hv)_j=(v_{j+1}-2v_j+v_{j-1})/h^2$. At the right endpoint define $(D_-v)_N=(v_N-v_{N-1})/h$. The interior inner product, norm, and edge inner product are
$$ \langle p,q\rangle_h=h\sum_{j=1}^{N-1}p_j\overline{q_j},\qquad \|v\|_h^2=\langle v,v\rangle_h,\qquad \langle p,q\rangle_{e,h}=h\sum_{j=0}^{N-1}(D_+p)_j\overline{(D_+q)_j}. $$
Dirichlet grid functions have prescribed endpoint values; when they are zero, the interior norm and edge inner product above are the ones used for the wave energy.

All statements below distinguish these periodic, infinite, and finite-interval index sets. Periodic Fourier calculations are not boundary estimates for the finite-interval grid.

## Definition

For [[def-age-structured-renewal-transport-problem]], input a finite horizon $T>0$, a cutoff $A>T$, integers $J,N\ge1$, and use the uniform grid $a_j=j\Delta a$ with $\Delta a=A/J$ and cells $C_j=[a_{j-1},a_j]$. Set $\Delta t=T/N$ and $t_k=k\Delta t$ for $0\le k\le N$. Use the model rates $\mu,\beta$ and input nonnegative initial cell masses $M_j^0$. Also input one positive-birth-quadrature setting for each cell as specified in [[alg-age-structured-positive-birth-quadrature]]; if omitted, use its default one-panel midpoint setting. Keep these settings fixed at every time step. Evaluate $\mu_j=\mu((a_{j-1}+a_j)/2)$. Require the transport-plus-loss CFL

$$\lambda+\Delta t\,\mu_\infty\le1,\qquad \lambda=\Delta t/\Delta a,\quad\mu_\infty=\|\mu\|_\infty.$$

If the CFL inequality fails, return status `invalid-cfl` without an update.

Initialize birth, quadrature-status, and outflow records as empty, and set cumulative outflow $O_h^0=0$. For each $k=0,\ldots,N-1$, put $u_j^k=M_j^k/\Delta a$, compute $B_h^k$ by calling [[alg-age-structured-positive-birth-quadrature]] with the current masses, model fertility $\beta$, and the selected cell settings, and set the upwind fluxes $F_0^k=B_h^k$ and $F_j^k=u_j^k$ for $1\le j\le J$. Update, for $1\le j\le J$,

$$M_j^{k+1}=M_j^k-\Delta t(F_j^k-F_{j-1}^k)-\Delta t\,\mu_jM_j^k.$$

The right flux $F_J^k$ is absorbing outflow: record and discard the step mass $\Delta t F_J^k$, set $O_h^{k+1}=O_h^k+\Delta t F_J^k$, and allow no inflow from ages above $A$. Append $B_h^k$, the quadrature status, and the step outflow record, then proceed to step $k+1$. Return $(M^k)_{k=0}^N$ with the birth, quadrature-status, step-outflow, and cumulative-outflow records. An invalid grid or failed rate/quadrature evaluation returns failure with no partial current step. A `cap-reached` adaptive quadrature estimate may be used for a finite step, but its status is retained and carries no accuracy claim.

## Definition

Use the uniform-grid indices, physical nodes, and spacings of [[def-uniform-grid-and-difference-operators]]. Fix a wave speed $c>0$, an interval length $L=Nh$ with $N\ge2$, and a time step $k>0$. Write $\nu=ck/h$. The target model is the real scalar wave equation $u_{tt}=c^2u_{xx}$, and grid states are real-valued. Prescribe a real initial displacement row $U^0$ and discrete initial-velocity row $V^0$, and set $U^1=U^0+kV^0$. For smooth Dirichlet data $u_0,u_1:[0,L]\to\mathbb R$ with $u_0(0)=u_0(L)=u_1(0)=u_1(L)=0$, the corresponding sample rows are $U_j^0=u_0(x_j)$ and $V_j^0=u_1(x_j)$; for smooth periodic data, take real $L$-periodic $u_0,u_1$ and sample them at $x_j$. In both cases the discrete initial velocity equals the sampled $u_1$. The centered leapfrog recurrence is
$$ U_j^{n+1}-2U_j^n+U_j^{n-1}=\nu^2(U_{j+1}^n-2U_j^n+U_{j-1}^n),\qquad n\ge1. $$
For the finite Dirichlet interval, require $U_0^0=U_N^0=V_0^0=V_N^0=0$ and impose the recurrence for $j=1,\ldots,N-1$, with $U_0^n=U_N^n=0$ for every $n\ge0$. For the periodic branch, use $j=0,\ldots,N-1$, reduce indices modulo $N$, and impose the recurrence at every node. Fourier analysis of this real periodic update uses its complex-linear extension to the complexified grid space. No convergence order for a particular initialization formula is asserted here.

## Definition

Use the index sets and uniform spacings of [[def-uniform-grid-and-difference-operators]]: $x_j=jh$, $j\in\mathbb Z$, or $j$ reduced modulo $N$ in the periodic case. Fix $a>0$, $h,k>0$, and $\nu=ak/h$. The target equation is the one-dimensional constant-velocity transport equation $u_t+a u_x=0$, the constant-coefficient case of [[def-linear-transport-equation-and-its-characteristic-flow]]. Set $U_j^0=u_0(jh)$ and define, for $n\ge0$,
$$ \begin{aligned} \text{upwind: }&U_j^{n+1}=U_j^n-\nu(U_j^n-U_{j-1}^n),\\ \text{downwind: }&U_j^{n+1}=U_j^n-\nu(U_{j+1}^n-U_j^n),\\ \text{centered: }&U_j^{n+1}=U_j^n-\frac{\nu}{2}(U_{j+1}^n-U_{j-1}^n),\\ \text{Lax--Friedrichs: }&U_j^{n+1}=\frac{U_{j-1}^n+U_{j+1}^n}{2}-\frac{\nu}{2}(U_{j+1}^n-U_{j-1}^n),\\ \text{Lax--Wendroff: }&U_j^{n+1}=U_j^n-\frac{\nu}{2}(U_{j+1}^n-U_{j-1}^n)+\frac{\nu^2}{2}(U_{j+1}^n-2U_j^n+U_{j-1}^n). \end{aligned} $$
On a periodic grid, every index in these formulas is reduced modulo $N$; no physical boundary data are present. For $a<0$, reflect the stencil by $j\mapsto-j$ and replace $\nu$ by $|a|k/h$.

For a finite interval $[0,L]$ with $a>0$, the inflow boundary is $x=0$. The upwind initial/boundary rows are $U_j^0=u_0(jh)$ for $j=0,\ldots,N$, $U_0^n=g(t_n)$ with $u_0(0)=g(0)$, and
$$ U_j^{n+1}=(1-\nu)U_j^n+\nu U_{j-1}^n,\qquad j=1,\ldots,N,\quad n\ge0. $$
The outflow node $j=N$ is computed by this row and receives no prescribed value. This item supplies no finite-interval boundary closure or stability statement for centered, Lax--Friedrichs, or Lax--Wendroff updates.

## Example

Let $N$ be even and consider the periodic centered leapfrog wave scheme. At $\nu=1$, its Nyquist mode has a repeated root $-1$ and admits linear-in-time growth unless the starting coefficient satisfies $w^1=-w^0$. The usual modified quadratic energy is semidefinite there and is indefinite for $\nu>1$.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** An even periodic grid of real-valued states, $\nu=ck/h>0$, and a Nyquist mode $\phi_{N/2}(j)=(-1)^j$.

[F1] The periodic wave recurrence is defined in [[def-centered-leapfrog-wave-scheme]].

[F2] At $\nu=1$ and even $N$, the periodic wave theorem gives the Nyquist root and compatibility condition ([[thm-periodic-centered-wave-amplification-and-endpoint]]).

[F3] The one-dimensional heat symbol with unit diffusivity gives $-\Delta_h\phi_\ell=4h^{-2}s_\ell\phi_\ell$ ([[lem-periodic-heat-difference-amplification-symbol]]).

[F4] The finite root-of-unity sum gives orthogonality of distinct Fourier modes ([[lem-orthogonality-of-characters-on-a-finite-cyclic-group]]).

[F5] The periodic grid norm is $\|v\|_{2,h}^2=h\sum_j|v_j|^2$ ([[def-uniform-grid-and-difference-operators]]).

[F6] The periodic forward-difference inner product is $\langle D_+p,D_+q\rangle_{e,h}=h\sum_j(D_+p)_j\overline{(D_+q)_j}$ ([[def-uniform-grid-and-difference-operators]]).

## Verification

1.1 For the Nyquist mode, $s_{N/2}=1$, so the recurrence polynomial is $r^2-2(1-2\nu^2)r+1$. At $\nu=1$ this is $(r+1)^2$, with solution $w_n=(-1)^n(A+nB)$; the coefficient $B$ vanishes exactly when $w^1=-w^0$. [F1, F2, algebra]

1.2 If $\nu>1$, then $q=1-2\nu^2<-1$. The roots of $r^2-2qr+1$ are real and negative because the discriminant is $4(q^2-1)>0$, their product is $1$, and their sum is $2q<-2$. Hence one root has modulus greater than one. [F1, algebra]

1.3 Define the periodic modified energy of adjacent states $X=U^n$, $Y=U^{n+1}$ by $$ \mathcal E_{\rm per}(Y,X)=\frac{1}{2k^2}\|Y-X\|_{2,h}^2+\frac{c^2}{2}\operatorname{Re}\langle D_+Y,D_+X\rangle_{e,h}. $$ For one normalized Fourier mode $\psi_\ell=\phi_\ell/\sqrt L$ with coefficients $x,y$, put $m=(x+y)/2$ and $v=(y-x)/k$. Reindexing the finite periodic sum gives $\langle D_+p,D_+q\rangle_{e,h}=\langle-\Delta_hp,q\rangle_{2,h}$. Thus [F3] gives $\|D_+\psi_\ell\|_{e,h}^2=4h^{-2}s_\ell$, while [F4] gives orthogonality; the $N$ nonzero orthogonal vectors form a basis of the $N$-dimensional space $\mathbb C^{J_N}$. By [F5] they are normalized by $\sqrt L$. Since $x=m-kv/2$ and $y=m+kv/2$, $\operatorname{Re}(y\overline{x})=|m|^2-k^2|v|^2/4$. Summing these diagonal contributions using [F6] gives the modal energy $$ \frac12(1-\nu^2s_\ell)|v|^2+2c^2h^{-2}s_\ell|m|^2. $$ At $\nu=1$, $0\le s_\ell\le1$, so every modal term is nonnegative, while the Nyquist velocity coefficient is zero. Orthogonal Fourier decomposition makes $\mathcal E_{\rm per}$ semidefinite. [F3, F4, F5, F6, algebra]

1.4 Set the real amplitude $A=1$ and take $X=A\phi_{N/2}$ and $Y=-X$. Then $X\ne0$, $\|Y-X\|^2=4\|X\|^2$, and $\langle D_+Y,D_+X\rangle_{e,h}=-4h^{-2}\|X\|^2$, so $$ \mathcal E_{\rm per}(-X,X)=\frac{2}{k^2}(1-\nu^2)\|X\|_{2,h}^2. $$ It is zero at $\nu=1$ and negative at $\nu>1$. [F3, F5, F6, algebra]

2.1 The state $(Y,X)=(0,X)$ has $\mathcal E_{\rm per}(0,X)=\|X\|_{2,h}^2/(2k^2)>0$. Together with step 1.4, this shows that the form is indefinite for $\nu>1$. [F5, step 1.4, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Let $N\ge2$, $h>0$, $L=Nh$, and let $w=(w_0,\ldots,w_N)$ be a complex grid function with $w_0=w_N=0$. Then
$$ \|w\|_h\le L\|D_+w\|_{e,h}. $$

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** A complex grid function $w$ on $j=0,\ldots,N$ with zero endpoint values.

[F1] The weighted interior and edge norms are those of [[def-uniform-grid-and-difference-operators]].

## Proof

1.1 For each $1\le j\le N-1$, put $d_i=w_{i+1}-w_i$ for $i=0,\ldots,j-1$. Expanding both expressions shows $$ j\sum_{i=0}^{j-1}|d_i|^2-\left|\sum_{i=0}^{j-1}d_i\right|^2 =\sum_{0\le i<r<j}|d_i-d_r|^2, $$ since each side equals $(j-1)\sum_i|d_i|^2-\sum_{i<r}(d_i\overline{d_r}+d_r\overline{d_i})$. The right side is nonnegative. Since $w_0=0$, $w_j=\sum_{i=0}^{j-1}d_i$, so $$ |w_j|^2\le j\sum_{i=0}^{j-1}|w_{i+1}-w_i|^2 \le N\sum_{i=0}^{N-1}|w_{i+1}-w_i|^2. $$ [given, F1, algebra]

2.1 Sum the step 1.1 bound over $j=1,\ldots,N-1$ and multiply by $h$. Since $(N-1)N h\le N^2h$ and $\|D_+w\|_{e,h}^2=h^{-1}\sum_{i=0}^{N-1}|w_{i+1}-w_i|^2$, we obtain $\|w\|_h^2\le N^2h^2\|D_+w\|_{e,h}^2=L^2\|D_+w\|_{e,h}^2$. Taking nonnegative square roots proves the claim. [step 1.1, F1, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Let $N\ge2$, $h>0$, and let $u=(u_0,\ldots,u_N)$ and $v=(v_0,\ldots,v_N)$ be complex grid functions. With the finite-interval inner products and differences of [[def-uniform-grid-and-difference-operators]],
$$ \langle u,-\Delta_hv\rangle_h =\langle D_+u,D_+v\rangle_{e,h}+u_0\overline{(D_+v)_0}-u_N\overline{(D_-v)_N}. $$
In particular, if $u_0=u_N=0$, the two boundary terms vanish. On the subspace of grid functions with zero endpoints, $-\Delta_h$ is self-adjoint and nonnegative in the interior grid inner product, with $\langle u,-\Delta_hu\rangle_h=\|D_+u\|_{e,h}^2$.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** $N\ge2$, $h>0$, and complex grid values $u_j,v_j$ on $j=0,\ldots,N$.

[F1] The interior and edge inner products and differences are defined in [[def-uniform-grid-and-difference-operators]].

## Proof

1.1 Put $d_j=v_j-v_{j-1}$ for $j=1,\ldots,N$. Expanding the second difference gives $$ \langle u,-\Delta_hv\rangle_h=-\frac1h\sum_{j=1}^{N-1}u_j\overline{(d_{j+1}-d_j)}. $$ Shift the index in the $d_{j+1}$ sum and telescope: $$ -\sum_{j=1}^{N-1}u_j\overline{(d_{j+1}-d_j)} =\sum_{j=1}^{N}(u_j-u_{j-1})\overline{d_j}+u_0\overline{d_1}-u_N\overline{d_N}. $$ Dividing by $h$ identifies the edge sum and boundary terms in the displayed identity. [F1, algebra]

2.1 When $u_0=u_N=0$, step 1.1 reduces to $\langle u,-\Delta_hv\rangle_h=\langle D_+u,D_+v\rangle_{e,h}$. Applying this identity after exchanging $u,v$ and taking complex conjugates gives $\langle-\Delta_hu,v\rangle_h=\langle u,-\Delta_hv\rangle_h$, so $-\Delta_h$ is self-adjoint on the zero-endpoint subspace. Setting $u=v$ gives $\langle u,-\Delta_hu\rangle_h=\|D_+u\|_{e,h}^2\ge0$. [step 1.1, F1] ∎

## Statement

Their squared moduli, in the same order, are
$$ 1-2\nu(1-\nu)(1-C_\ell),\quad 1+2\nu(1+\nu)(1-C_\ell),\quad 1+\nu^2S_\ell^2,\quad 1-(1-\nu^2)S_\ell^2,\quad 1-\nu^2(1-\nu^2)(1-C_\ell)^2. $$
The $N$ Fourier vectors form an orthogonal basis under the periodic inner product of [[def-uniform-grid-and-difference-operators]], and each has squared norm $Nh$.

**Given:** $N\ge2$, $a,h,k>0$, and the periodic stencils of [[def-periodic-one-way-advection-schemes]].

[F1] The five one-step formulas and periodic wrap are defined in [[def-periodic-one-way-advection-schemes]].

[F2] The finite root-of-unity sum $\sum_{j=0}^{N-1}\exp(2\pi i(\ell-r)j/N)$ equals $N$ if $\ell\equiv r\pmod N$ and $0$ otherwise ([[lem-orthogonality-of-characters-on-a-finite-cyclic-group]]).

[F5] The periodic grid inner product and norm are $\langle p,q\rangle_{2,h}=h\sum_jp_j\overline{q_j}$ and $\|p\|_{2,h}^2=h\sum_j|p_j|^2$ ([[def-uniform-grid-and-difference-operators]]).

1.1 Write $\phi_j=z_\ell^j$. Then $\phi_{j+1}=z_\ell\phi_j$, $\phi_{j-1}=z_\ell^{-1}\phi_j$, and $z_\ell^{-1}=\bar z_\ell$. ## Statement

Fix $a,T>0$. The following two claims hold.

**Strict domain-of-dependence obstruction.** Suppose $h_m,k_m\to0$ and along a subsequence $ak_m/h_m\ge1+\varepsilon$ for some fixed $\varepsilon>0$, and put $R=aT\varepsilon/(4(1+\varepsilon))$. Consider any homogeneous linear nearest-neighbor explicit update on the infinite grid whose value after $n$ steps depends only on initial indices $j-n,\ldots,j+n$. Fix a real-valued datum $u_0\in C_c^\infty((-R,R);\mathbb R)$ with $u_0(0)=1$ and initialize each mesh by $U_j^0=u_0(jh_m)$. The exact samples $u_0(jh_m-at_m)$ and numerical values fail to converge in the sampled maximum error
$$\sup_{j\in\mathbb Z}|U_j^{n_m}-u_0(jh_m-at_m)|$$
at $t_m=n_mk_m\to T$, where $n_m=\lfloor T/k_m\rfloor$.

**CFL insufficiency for centered advection.** For any fixed period $P>0$, set $N_q=4q$, $h_q=P/N_q$, and $k_q=h_q/(2a)$ for $q\ge1$. Let $Q_q$ be the centered advection update on this periodic grid and $r_q=\lfloor T/k_q\rfloor$. Then $0<ak_q/h_q=1/2<1$, but
$$\max_{\substack{r\in\mathbb N\\0\le r k_q\le T}}\|Q_q^r\|_{2,h_q\to2,h_q}\ge\|Q_q^{r_q}\|_{2,h_q\to2,h_q}\ge(\sqrt5/2)^{r_q}\longrightarrow\infty.$$
Thus a fixed strict violation of $ak/h\le1$ prevents convergence for the nearest-neighbor family, while the domain-of-dependence bound does not suffice for uniform finite-time power stability of every periodic nearest-neighbor scheme.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Fixed $a,T>0$; for the first claim, an infinite-grid homogeneous linear nearest-neighbor update and a mesh subsequence with $ak/h\ge1+\varepsilon$; and, independently, for the second claim, the fixed-period centered periodic family with $N_q=4q$.

[F1] The centered advection stencil in [[def-periodic-one-way-advection-schemes]] is a homogeneous explicit nearest-neighbor update.

[F2] For a real-valued $C^1$ function on an open subset of $\mathbb R^2$, the first coordinate partial derivatives exist and are continuous; a classical solution on a neighborhood of a characteristic segment is continuous on that segment ([[def-ck-and-multi-index-notation-in-several-variables]]).

[F3] Finite induction on the natural-number step count is valid ([[thm-induction-principle]]).

[F4] There is a real cutoff $\chi\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R)$ with $\chi=1$ for $|x|\le1$ and $\chi=0$ for $|x|\ge2$ ([[lem-schwartz-cutoffs-from-the-standard-smooth-step]]).

[F5] For constant velocity $a$, the characteristic ODE is $X'(s)=a$ with terminal value $X(t)=x$, and the transport equation is $u_t+a u_x=0$ ([[def-linear-transport-equation-and-its-characteristic-flow]]).

[F6] A real differentiable function with zero derivative on an interval is constant there, by the mean value theorem ([[cor-mean-value-theorem]]).

[F7] For every real $y$ there is a unique integer $m=\lfloor y\rfloor$ with $m\le y<m+1$ ([[lem-integer-part]]).

[F8] For an open interval $I$, $C_c^\infty(I;\mathbb C)$ consists of smooth functions whose support is a compact subset of $I$; its real-valued functions form the real test-function subspace ([[def-test-function-space-d-of-an-open-set]]).

[F9] On a periodic grid, the centered advection factor is $g_{\rm centered}=1-i\nu S_\ell$, where $z_\ell=e^{2\pi i\ell/N}$ and $S_\ell=\operatorname{Im}z_\ell$; the modes form an orthogonal basis ([[lem-periodic-advection-amplification-symbols]]).

[F10] The operator norm is the supremum of $\|Qv\|$ over the unit ball in the given norm ([[def-operator-norm]]).

[F11] The periodic grid has indices modulo $N$ and norm $\|v\|_{2,h}^2=h\sum_{j=0}^{N-1}|v_j|^2$ ([[def-uniform-grid-and-difference-operators]]).

## Proof

1.1 Put $R=aT\varepsilon/(4(1+\varepsilon))$ and take $\chi$ from [F4]. Set $u_0(x)=\chi(3x/R)$. Then $u_0$ is smooth, equals $1$ at zero, and is supported in $[-2R/3,2R/3]$, a compact subset of $(-R,R)$; by [F8] it is an admissible real-valued datum. [given, F4, F8, algebra]

1.2 By finite induction [F3], the value at index $j$ after zero steps depends only on $j$. If every value after $n$ steps depends only on initial indices $j-n,\ldots,j+n$, then the next update reads indices $j-1,j,j+1$ at time $n$, whose initial dependence intervals have union $[j-(n+1),j+(n+1)]$. Thus after $n$ steps only initial indices $j-n,\ldots,j+n$ can affect the value. [given, F3, induction]

2.1 Along the violating subsequence put $n_m=\lfloor T/k_m\rfloor$ and $j_m=\lfloor aT/h_m+1/2\rfloor$. By [F7], $j_m\le aT/h_m+1/2<j_m+1$, so $|j_mh_m-aT|\le h_m/2$. Hence every sampled initial value on which $U_{j_m}^{n_m}$ depends is zero, so $U_{j_m}^{n_m}=0$. [given, F7, step 1.1, step 1.2, algebra]

3.1 The constant-velocity characteristic is $X(s;t,x)=x+a(s-t)$: it has derivative $a$ and terminal value $x$, and any other solution agrees by [F6] applied to its difference from $X$. The explicit function $u^*(y,s)=u_0(y-as)$ has partial derivatives $u^*_y=u_0'(y-as)$ and $u^*_s=-a u_0'(y-as)$ by one-variable difference quotients, so it solves $u_t+a u_x=0$ with initial data $u_0$. To verify uniqueness, let $u$ be any classical solution on an open neighborhood of this characteristic segment with the same initial data, fix $(x,t)$, and set $v(s)=u(x+a(s-t),s)$ on $[0,t]$. For interior $s$ and small nonzero $\delta$ whose coordinate segments remain in the solution domain, applying [F6] separately in the first and second coordinates gives $$\frac{v(s+\delta)-v(s)}{\delta}=a u_x(\xi_\delta,s+\delta)+u_t(x+a(s-t),\eta_\delta),$$ where $\xi_\delta$ lies between $x+a(s-t)$ and $x+a(s+\delta-t)$, and $\eta_\delta$ lies between $s$ and $s+\delta$. As $\delta\to0$, these intermediate points tend to $(x+a(s-t),s)$, so continuity of the partials in [F2] yields $v'(s)=a u_x(x+a(s-t),s)+u_t(x+a(s-t),s)=0$. Then [F6] makes $v$ constant, hence $u(x,t)=u_0(x-at)$. Since $0\le T-n_mk_m<k_m$ and $k_m\to0$, the exact characteristic foot $j_mh_m-a n_mk_m$ tends to $aT-aT=0$. By continuity and $u_0(0)=1$, the exact sample tends to $1$, while step 2.1 gives numerical value zero. Thus the sampled maximum error does not tend to zero. [F2, F5, F6, step 1.1, step 2.1, algebra]

4.1 For the separate centered-family claim, fix $P>0$ and use $N_q=4q$, $h_q=P/(4q)$, $k_q=h_q/(2a)$, and $r_q=\lfloor T/k_q\rfloor$. Then [F1] gives the centered update with $ak_q/h_q=1/2$, and the Fourier index $\ell=q$ is admissible with $z_\ell=\exp(2\pi i q/(4q))=i$. By [F9] its multiplier is $g=1-i/2$, so $|g|=\sqrt5/2>1$. Repeated application gives $Q_q^{r_q}\phi_q=g^{r_q}\phi_q$. The mode is nonzero, and the finite Fourier basis in [F9] diagonalizes $Q_q^{r_q}$ with finitely many finite multipliers, so this operator is bounded. By [F10] its norm is at least $|g|^{r_q}$. Since [F7] gives $r_q\ge T/k_q-1=8aTq/P-1\to\infty$, these norms are unbounded while all time levels satisfy $r_qk_q\le T$. Thus the domain-of-dependence bound is not sufficient for uniform finite-time power stability. [given, F1, F7, F9, F10, F11, algebra] ∎

## Statement

On a periodic grid of length $L=Nh$, let $\nu=ck/h>0$, $V^0=(U^1-U^0)/k$, and write $U^n=\sum_{\ell=0}^{N-1}w_\ell^n\phi_\ell$ in the discrete Fourier basis; write $\widehat V_\ell^0$ for the coefficient of $V^0$ in the same basis. Then
$$ w_\ell^{n+1}-2(1-2\nu^2s_\ell)w_\ell^n+w_\ell^{n-1}=0,\qquad s_\ell=\sin^2(\pi\ell/N). $$
For $0<\nu\le\nu_0<1$, the nonconstant roots are distinct and have modulus one, and
$$ \|U^n\|_{2,h}\le\left(1+\frac{\nu_0}{\sqrt{1-\nu_0^2}}\right)\|U^0\|_{2,h}+t_n\|V^0\|_{2,h}. $$
The mean mode is $w_0^n=w_0^0+t_n\widehat V_0^0$. At $\nu=1$ and even $N$, the Nyquist mode has the repeated root $-1$ and solution $w_{N/2}^n=(-1)^n(A+nB)$, where $B=0$ exactly when $w_{N/2}^1=-w_{N/2}^0$. Thus arbitrary starting pairs do not have a uniform endpoint power bound.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** $N\ge2$, fixed $L=Nh$, $c,h,k>0$, and the periodic centered leapfrog scheme.

[F1] The periodic branch obeys $U_j^{n+1}-2U_j^n+U_j^{n-1}=\nu^2(U_{j+1}^n-2U_j^n+U_{j-1}^n)$ ([[def-centered-leapfrog-wave-scheme]]).

[F2] The one-dimensional specialization of the periodic heat symbol lemma with unit diffusivity gives $-\Delta_h\phi_\ell=4h^{-2}s_\ell\phi_\ell$ ([[lem-periodic-heat-difference-amplification-symbol]]).

[F3] The displayed periodic Fourier modes form a basis of the complexified grid space ([[lem-periodic-heat-difference-amplification-symbol]]).

[F4] The finite root-of-unity sum gives orthogonality of distinct periodic Fourier modes ([[lem-orthogonality-of-characters-on-a-finite-cyclic-group]]).

[F5] Complex conjugation and modulus have their coordinate, multiplication, and triangle laws ([[def-complex-conjugate-real-imaginary-part-and-modulus]], [[lem-complex-conjugation-and-modulus-laws]]).

[F6] The periodic grid norm is $\|v\|_{2,h}^2=h\sum_j|v_j|^2$ ([[def-uniform-grid-and-difference-operators]]).

## Proof

1.1 Substituting one mode from [F2] into [F1] uses $-\Delta_h\phi_\ell=4h^{-2}s_\ell\phi_\ell$ and gives the displayed scalar recurrence, whose characteristic polynomial is $$ p_\ell(r)=r^2-2(1-2\nu^2s_\ell)r+1. $$ [F1, F2, algebra]

2.1 For $\ell=0$, $s_0=0$, so successive first differences are constant and $w_0^n=w_0^0+n(w_0^1-w_0^0)=w_0^0+t_n\widehat V_0^0$. For $\ell\ne0$ and $\nu<1$, put $q=1-2\nu^2s_\ell$; then $-1<q<1$, and $\rho=q+i\sqrt{1-q^2}$ and $\bar\rho$ are distinct roots with modulus one. [F5, step 1.1, algebra]

2.2 For a nonconstant mode the recurrence solution matching $w_\ell^0,w_\ell^1$ is $$ w_\ell^n=w_\ell^0\frac{\rho^n+\bar\rho^n}{2}+(w_\ell^1-qw_\ell^0)\frac{\rho^n-\bar\rho^n}{\rho-\bar\rho}. $$ Indeed both sequences solve the recurrence and the right side equals $w_\ell^0,w_\ell^1$ at $n=0,1$. The quotient is $\sum_{r=0}^{n-1}\rho^{n-1-r}\bar\rho^r$, so its modulus is at most $n$. Also $|(\rho^n-\bar\rho^n)/(\rho-\bar\rho)|\le1/\sqrt{1-q^2}$ since $|\rho^n-\bar\rho^n|\le2$ and $|\rho-\bar\rho|=2\sqrt{1-q^2}$. [step 1.1, F5, algebra]

3.1 Since $w_\ell^1-qw_\ell^0=k\widehat V_\ell^0+(1-q)w_\ell^0$ and $$ \frac{1-q}{\sqrt{1-q^2}}=\frac{\nu\sqrt{s_\ell}}{\sqrt{1-\nu^2s_\ell}}\le\frac{\nu_0}{\sqrt{1-\nu_0^2}}, $$ step 2.2 gives $|w_\ell^n|\le(1+\nu_0/\sqrt{1-\nu_0^2})|w_\ell^0|+t_n|\widehat V_\ell^0|$. The same bound holds for the mean mode. [F2, step 2.2, algebra]

4.1 The modes are a basis by [F3] and orthogonal by [F4]. By [F6], each has squared norm $Nh$, so Parseval's identity holds in $\|\cdot\|_{2,h}$. Squaring the coefficient bounds, summing, and using $$ \left(\sum_\ell a_\ell b_\ell\right)^2\le\left(\sum_\ell a_\ell^2\right)\left(\sum_\ell b_\ell^2\right), $$ which follows by expanding $\sum_{\ell<r}(a_\ell b_r-a_rb_\ell)^2\ge0$, yields the stated weighted-grid norm estimate. [F3, F4, F5, F6, step 3.1, algebra]

5.1 If $\nu=1$, $N$ is even, and $\ell=N/2$, then $s_\ell=1$ and $p_\ell(r)=(r+1)^2$. Its solutions are $(-1)^n(A+nB)$; the initial values give $B=-w_\ell^1-w_\ell^0$, so $B=0$ exactly when $w_\ell^1=-w_\ell^0$. For $B\ne0$ the mode grows linearly in $n$, proving the endpoint caveat. [F1, step 1.1, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Let $n_0\ge0$ belong to $BV(0,\infty)\cap L^1(0,\infty)$, where $BV$ means finite total variation, and let $\mu,\beta$ be bounded nonnegative Lipschitz rates. Fix a finite horizon $T>0$. Initialize the finite-volume scheme with exact cell masses $M_j^0=\int_{C_j}n_0(a)\,da$. Assume every positive birth-quadrature evaluation succeeds and the quadrature rule settings are fixed over time. The compatibility between the one-sided initial trace and the renewal birth rate is not assumed. For any sequence of age cutoffs $A_m\to\infty$ with $A_m>T$ for all sufficiently large $m$, and admissible uniform grids with integers $J_m,N_m\ge1$, $A_m=J_m\Delta a_m$ and $T=N_m\Delta t_m$, assume $\Delta a_m,\Delta t_m>0$ and $\Delta a_m,\Delta t_m\to0$, $\Delta t_m/\Delta a_m\in[c_-,c_+]$ for fixed positive bounds, and the transport-plus-loss CFL; extend the cellwise-constant reconstructions by zero above each cutoff. Linear interpolation between time levels then converges to the mild solution in $C([0,T];L^1(0,\infty))$. This is an $L^1$ convergence statement; it asserts no smooth Taylor error rate.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The BV initial density, bounded Lipschitz rates, and the finite-volume update in [[def-age-structured-renewal-transport-problem]] and [[alg-age-structured-renewal-upwind-finite-volume]].

[F1] [[def-age-structured-renewal-transport-problem]]: a weak solution is continuous in time with values in L1 and satisfies the displayed test-function identity, initial trace and renewal birth relation.

[F2] [[thm-age-structured-renewal-characteristic-solution]]: the characteristic formula and Volterra equation have a unique mild solution.

[F3] [[alg-age-structured-renewal-upwind-finite-volume]]: the cell update is the explicit flux balance; birth weights are nonnegative, supported in each cell and sum to the cell width; the right boundary is absorbing.

[F4] [[thm-age-structured-renewal-upwind-positivity-mass-bound-and-stability]]: discrete masses stay nonnegative and their total is at most $1+\Delta t\beta_\infty$ times the preceding total.

1.1 Write $u_j^k=M_j^k/\Delta a$, $B_k=B_h^k$, $\lambda=\Delta t/\Delta a$, and $V_k=|u_1^k-B_k|+\sum_{j=2}^{J}|u_j^k-u_{j-1}^k|$. The initial cell averages satisfy $V_0\le\operatorname{TV}(n_0)+\|n_0\|_\infty+\beta_\infty\|n_0\|_1$, which is finite because an integrable function of finite total variation on the half-line has finite essential supremum; the first term bounds differences of adjacent cell averages by averaging the variation measure. 2.1 Set $u_0^k=B_k$ and put $d_1^k=u_1^k-B_k$ and $d_j^k=u_j^k-u_{j-1}^k$ for $2\le j\le J$. The quadrature weights are fixed and nonnegative, so $|B_{k+1}-B_k|\le\beta_\infty\sum_j|M_j^{k+1}-M_j^k|$. Adding the first-cell bound to the preceding sum combines the $d_1^k$ coefficients as $(1-\lambda-\Delta t\mu_1)+\lambda\le1$; all other variation coefficients are at most $1$. 3.1 Iterating [F4] gives $N_k\le(1+\Delta t\beta_\infty)^kN_0\le e^{k\Delta t\beta_\infty}N_0\le e^{\beta_\infty T}N_0$. ## Statement

Let $A>T$ and let $n_0\ge0$ be integrable. For an initial cohort of age $a$, its survival through duration $s$ satisfies

$$e^{-\|\mu\|_\infty s}\le S(a,s)\le e^{-\mu_*s},\qquad \mu_*:=\operatorname*{ess\,inf}_{r\ge0}\mu(r).$$

No cohort born during $[0,T]$ reaches age $A$. The exact number of initial individuals that exits through age $A$ by time $t\le T$ is

$$O_A(t)=\int_{A-t}^{A}n_0(a)S(a,A-a)\,da\le\int_{A-T}^{\infty}n_0(a)\,da.$$

Let $n^A$ be the finite-age solution from [[thm-age-structured-renewal-finite-cutoff-characteristic-solution]] with initial data $n_0^A=n_0\mathbf 1_{[0,A]}$, extended by zero above $A$. Then

$$\sup_{0\le t\le T}\|n(t)-n^A(t)\|_1\le2e^{\beta_\infty T}\int_{A-T}^{\infty}n_0(a)\,da.$$

Under the smooth discretization hypotheses of [[thm-age-structured-renewal-smooth-first-order-convergence]], let $u_h^k$ be its piecewise-constant reconstruction, extended by zero above $A$. At every time level,

$$\|u_h^k-n(t_k,\cdot)\|_1\le2e^{\beta_\infty T}\int_{A-T}^{\infty}n_0(a)\,da+C_T(\Delta a+\Delta t+\epsilon_Q).$$

**Given:** The infinite-age model and mild solution from [[def-age-structured-renewal-transport-problem]] and [[thm-age-structured-renewal-characteristic-solution]], with nonnegative initial density and $A>T$.

[F1] [[def-age-structured-renewal-transport-problem]]: a cohort of age $a$ follows $a(s)=a+s$ and survives for duration $s$ by $S(a,s)$.

[F2] [[thm-age-structured-renewal-characteristic-solution]]: the infinite-age mild solution is unique and is given by characteristics and its birth-rate Volterra equation.

[F3] [[thm-age-structured-renewal-finite-cutoff-characteristic-solution]]: the absorbing finite-age solution is unique and has mass at most $e^{\beta_\infty t}$ times its initial mass.

[F4] [[thm-age-structured-renewal-semigroup-growth-and-data-stability]]: infinite-age solutions with the same rates differ in $L^1$ by at most $e^{\beta_\infty t}$ times the difference in initial data.

[F5] [[thm-age-structured-renewal-smooth-first-order-convergence]]: for the exact finite-age solution, the numerical cell-mass error is bounded separately by $C_T(\Delta a+\Delta t+\epsilon_Q)$.

## Statement

Assume $n^A$ extends to $C^2([0,T]\times[0,A])$. Its smoothness at the renewal corner includes $n_0^A(0)=B_A(0)$ and $-(n_0^A)'(0)-\mu(0)n_0^A(0)=B_A'(0)$; no boundary value is imposed at the absorbing outflow. Take integers $J,N\ge1$, set $\Delta a=A/J$ and $\Delta t=T/N$, and use the corresponding uniform age and time grids. Initialize with exact cell masses and use the one-panel midpoint rule in each cell from [[alg-age-structured-positive-birth-quadrature]]. Assume $\Delta t/\Delta a\in[c_-,c_+]$ for fixed $0<c_-\le c_+<\infty$ and the transport-plus-loss CFL. Define

$$\epsilon_Q:=\max_{0\le k<N}\left|B_h(\overline M(t_k))-\int_0^A\beta(a)n^A(t_k,a)\,da\right|,$$

where $B_h(\overline M(t_k))$ is the birth-rate quadrature applied to the exact cell-average masses $\overline M_j(t_k)=\int_{C_j}n^A(t_k,a)\,da$. Then the cell-mass error $E_k=\sum_j|M_j^k-\int_{C_j}n^A(t_k,a)\,da|$ obeys

$$\max_{0\le k\le N}E_k\le C_T(\Delta a+\Delta t+\epsilon_Q).$$

The piecewise-constant reconstruction $u_h^k=M_j^k/\Delta a$ on cell $C_j$ and zero above $A$ satisfies the same $L^1$ error order. For the midpoint rule, $\epsilon_Q\le C_T\Delta a$ under the stated regularity, so the method is first order in age mesh and time step. If the capped adaptive rule is used instead, the estimate requires an independently established true $\epsilon_Q$; its reported indicator is not substituted for that hypothesis.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The smooth finite-cutoff solution and finite-volume scheme from [[def-age-structured-renewal-finite-cutoff-model]], [[thm-age-structured-renewal-finite-cutoff-characteristic-solution]] and [[alg-age-structured-renewal-upwind-finite-volume]], under the hypotheses in the Statement.

[F1] [[def-age-structured-renewal-finite-cutoff-model]]: $n_t+n_a=-\mu n$ on $0<a<A$, the renewal inflow is $B_A(t)=\int_0^A\beta(a)n^A(t,a)\,da$, and the upper boundary is absorbing outflow.

[F2] [[thm-age-structured-renewal-finite-cutoff-characteristic-solution]]: $n^A$ follows characteristics, satisfies the renewal relation, and its exact initial-cohort outflow is absorbing.

[F3] [[alg-age-structured-renewal-upwind-finite-volume]]: the cell-mass step is $M_j^{k+1}=M_j^k-\Delta t(F_j^k-F_{j-1}^k)-\Delta t\mu_jM_j^k$ with upwind face fluxes and absorbing top outflow.

[F4] [[thm-age-structured-renewal-upwind-positivity-mass-bound-and-stability]]: for the same coefficients and positive quadrature, a one-step mass difference is amplified by at most $1+\Delta t\beta_\infty$.

[F5] [[thm-composite-midpoint-error-bound]]: for $f\in C^2[a,b]$, the composite midpoint error on width $h$ is at most $(b-a)h^2\max|f''|/24$.

[F6] [[lem-discrete-one-step-error-recurrence-bound]]: if $e_0\le C_0h$ and $e_{k+1}\le(1+Lh)e_k+Ch^2$ on a fixed grid $Nh=T$, then $\max_ke_k\le C_T h$.

The smooth finite-age characteristic solution [F2] satisfies the transport equation and renewal boundary in [F1]. Integrating [F1] over one cell and one time step gives $\overline M_j(t_{k+1})=\overline M_j(t_k)-\int_{t_k}^{t_{k+1}}[n^A(s,a_j)-n^A(s,a_{j-1})]ds-\int_{t_k}^{t_{k+1}}\int_{C_j}\mu(a)n^A(s,a)\,da\,ds$, with $n^A(s,a_0)=B_A(s)$ and the outgoing trace at $a_J=A$. [F1, F2, construct, algebra]

2.1 Taylor's formula in age gives $\overline u_j(t)-n^A(t,a_j)=-\frac{\Delta a}{2}(n^A)_a(t,a_j)+O(\Delta a^2)$ uniformly. For interior cells, subtracting adjacent face-flux errors cancels the leading term and leaves $O((\Delta a)^2)$ per cell because $(n^A)_{aa}$ is bounded. In the first and last cells there is only one uncancelled endpoint face error, of size $O(\Delta a)$; these two cells contribute $O(\Delta t\Delta a)$ in total. Taylor's formula in time gives a face-integral remainder $O(\Delta t^2\Delta a)$ per cell after adjacent differences, using bounded $(n^A)_{ta}$, hence $O(\Delta t^2)$ after summing. At the inlet, the smooth trace gives $(n^A)_t(t,a_0)=B_A'(t)$, so the time derivative of $n^A(t,a_1)-B_A(t)$ is also bounded by $\Delta a\|(n^A)_{ta}\|_\infty$; thus the boundary birth flux has no additional O(\Delta t^2) term beyond this face remainder and $\Delta t\epsilon_Q$. For the reaction term, first note that $\overline u_j(t)=n^A(t,a_j^c)+O((\Delta a)^2)$ by the symmetric cell average. Summing and multiplying by $\Delta t$ gives $O(\Delta t(\Delta a)^2)$. Freezing the reaction term at $t_k$ instead of integrating in time contributes $O(\Delta t^2)$ after summing cells, since $(\mu n^A)_t$ is bounded. ## Statement

For the bounded fertility rate in the age model, write $\beta_\infty:=\|\beta\|_\infty$. Whenever [[alg-age-structured-positive-birth-quadrature]] returns an estimate for nonnegative cell masses and a bounded nonnegative fertility rate with upper bound $\beta_\infty$, its birth value satisfies $0\le B_h\le\beta_\infty\sum_jM_j$.

In the update of [[alg-age-structured-renewal-upwind-finite-volume]], suppose the initial masses are nonnegative, the CFL holds, and each cell quadrature has nonnegative weights summing to $\Delta a$. Then all updated masses remain nonnegative and, with $N_h^k=\sum_{j=1}^J M_j^k$,

$$N_h^{k+1}\le(1+\Delta t\,\beta_\infty)N_h^k.$$

For two runs with the same grid, rates and quadrature rule but different nonnegative initial mass vectors $M^0,\widetilde M^0$, the one-step difference satisfies

$$\|M^{k+1}-\widetilde M^{k+1}\|_{\ell^1}\le(1+\Delta t\,\beta_\infty)\|M^k-\widetilde M^k\|_{\ell^1}.$$

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The age model, positive birth quadrature and finite-volume update in [[def-age-structured-renewal-transport-problem]], [[alg-age-structured-positive-birth-quadrature]] and [[alg-age-structured-renewal-upwind-finite-volume]].

[F1] [[alg-age-structured-positive-birth-quadrature]]: each cell quadrature has nonnegative weights with total weight $\Delta a$, so its birth contribution is nonnegative and at most $\beta_\infty M_j$.

[F2] [[alg-age-structured-renewal-upwind-finite-volume]]: $M_j^{k+1}=M_j^k-\Delta t(F_j^k-F_{j-1}^k)-\Delta t\mu_jM_j^k$, with $F_0^k=B_h^k$, $F_j^k=M_j^k/\Delta a$ for $j\ge1$, and $\Delta t/\Delta a+\Delta t\mu_\infty\le1$.

[A1] The initial masses in both runs are nonnegative, and both runs use the same rates and positive quadrature rule.

## Proof

1.1 In midpoint mode, each of the $q_j$ samples has weight $\Delta a/q_j>0$, so the weights sum to the cell width. In capped-adaptive mode, every returned estimate is a finite sum of Simpson panel estimates on its leaf intervals; a two-panel Simpson block has weights proportional to $(1,4,1)$, all positive, and their sum is the block width. The leaf intervals partition the cell, so the combined weights are nonnegative and sum to its width, including when a cap is reached. Hence the cell contribution lies between $0$ and $u_j\beta_\infty\Delta a=\beta_\infty M_j$, and summing over cells gives the stated birth bound. A failure returns no estimate. [F1, construct, algebra]

1.2 Substituting $F_j^k=M_j^k/\Delta a$ in [F2] gives $M_1^{k+1}=(1-\lambda-\Delta t\mu_1)M_1^k+\Delta t B_h^k$ and, for $j\ge2$, $M_j^{k+1}=(1-\lambda-\Delta t\mu_j)M_j^k+\lambda M_{j-1}^k$. 2.1 Summing [F2] over cells telescopes the fluxes to $F_J^k-F_0^k$, hence $N_h^{k+1}=N_h^k-\Delta t F_J^k+\Delta t B_h^k-\Delta t\sum_j\mu_jM_j^k$. ## Statement

For the homogeneous Dirichlet recurrence of [[def-centered-leapfrog-wave-scheme]], let $0<\nu=ck/h<1$, $V^n=(U^{n+1}-U^n)/k$, and $\bar U^n=(U^{n+1}+U^n)/2$. Define
$$ E^{n+1/2}=\frac12\|V^n\|_h^2+\frac{c^2}{2}\langle D_+U^{n+1},D_+U^n\rangle_{e,h}. $$
Then $E^{n+1/2}$ is independent of $n$ and
$$ E^{n+1/2}\ge\frac{1-\nu^2}{2}\|V^n\|_h^2+\frac{c^2}{2}\|D_+\bar U^n\|_{e,h}^2. $$
Consequently it is a positive quadratic form on adjacent zero-boundary states. For mesh families with fixed wave speed $c>0$, fixed interval length $L$, and $\nu\le\nu_0<1$, it controls the interior state and its discrete velocity with constants independent of $h$.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** A fixed wave speed $c>0$, mesh sizes $h,k>0$, homogeneous Dirichlet endpoint values, and the source-free centered leapfrog recurrence.

[F1] The recurrence is $\delta_t^2U^n=c^2\Delta_hU^n$, with $U_0^n=U_N^n=0$ ([[def-centered-leapfrog-wave-scheme]]).

[F2] For zero endpoint values, $\langle u,-\Delta_hv\rangle_h=\langle D_+u,D_+v\rangle_{e,h}$; this is symmetric in $u,v$ ([[lem-dirichlet-grid-summation-by-parts]]).

2.1 For any zero-endpoint grid function $v$, $(v_{j+1}-v_j)^2\le2v_{j+1}^2+2v_j^2$ and summing over edges gives $$ \|D_+v\|_{e,h}^2=\frac1h\sum_{j=0}^{N-1}(v_{j+1}-v_j)^2\le\frac4{h^2}\|v\|_h^2. $$ Apply this to $V^n$, and use $\nu=ck/h$, in step 1.1 to obtain the asserted lower bound. 3.1 A zero-endpoint grid function with $D_+w=0$ is constant across all edges and therefore zero. Hence step 2.1 shows $E^{n+1/2}=0$ only when $V^n=0$ and $\bar U^n=0$, equivalently $U^{n+1}=U^n=0$. ## Statement

For the periodic schemes of [[def-periodic-one-way-advection-schemes]] with $a>0$, upwind powers are contractions in $\|\cdot\|_{2,h}$ for $0\le\nu\le1$ and grow for $\nu>1$. Lax--Friedrichs and Lax--Wendroff powers are contractions for $|\nu|\le1$; when $|\nu|>1$, Lax--Wendroff grows for $N\ge2$ and Lax--Friedrichs grows for $N\ge3$ (the $N=2$ Lax--Friedrichs stencil aliases its nonconstant mode). Downwind powers grow for every $\nu>0$ and $N\ge2$. Centered powers grow for every $\nu\ne0$ when $N\ge3$, while the $N=2$ centered stencil aliases to the identity. Reflection gives the same assertions for $a<0$ with $|\nu|$.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** A finite periodic grid with $N\ge2$, fixed $a>0$, $h,k>0$, and the exact amplification formulas.

[F1] The $N$ periodic Fourier vectors form an orthogonal basis ([[lem-periodic-advection-amplification-symbols]]).

[F2] The five amplification factors and squared moduli are those of [[lem-periodic-advection-amplification-symbols]].

[F3] The five periodic updates and their indexing are defined in [[def-periodic-one-way-advection-schemes]].

[F4] For a bounded linear map, its operator norm is the supremum of $\|Tx\|$ over the unit ball ([[def-operator-norm]]).

[F5] For $z=C+iS$ with $|z|=1$, one has $C^2+S^2=1$ and hence $1-C\ge0$, $0\le S^2\le1$; complex conjugation and modulus obey their field laws ([[def-complex-conjugate-real-imaginary-part-and-modulus]], [[lem-complex-conjugation-and-modulus-laws]]).

## Proof

1.1 By [F5], $1-C_\ell\ge0$ and $0\le S_\ell^2\le1$. Thus for $0\le\nu\le1$, the upwind formula gives $|g_{\rm up}|^2\le1$; for $|\nu|\le1$, the Lax--Friedrichs formula gives $|g_{\rm LF}|^2\le1$, and the Lax--Wendroff formula gives $|g_{\rm LW}|^2\le1$. [F2, F3, F5, algebra]

1.2 If $\nu>1$, every nonconstant mode has $C_\ell<1$, so $|g_{\rm up}|^2=1+2\nu(\nu-1)(1-C_\ell)>1$. If $|\nu|>1$ and $N\ge2$, the Lax--Wendroff mode $\ell=1$ has $C_\ell<1$ and $|g_{\rm LW}|^2=1+\nu^2(\nu^2-1)(1-C_\ell)^2>1$. For Lax--Friedrichs with $|\nu|>1$ and $N\ge3$, some mode has $S_\ell\ne0$, so $|g_{\rm LF}|^2=1+(\nu^2-1)S_\ell^2>1$. Downwind has $|g_{\rm down}|^2>1$ for each nonconstant mode whenever $\nu>0$. Centered has $|g_{\rm centered}|^2>1$ on any mode with $S_\ell\ne0$, which exists exactly when $N\ge3$. [F2, F3, F5, algebra]

2.1 Write an arbitrary vector as $v=\sum_\ell c_\ell\psi_\ell$ in the orthonormal Fourier basis [F1]. The $m$-step update sends it to $\sum_\ell c_\ell g_\ell^m\psi_\ell$, so $\|T^mv\|_{2,h}^2=\sum_\ell|c_\ell|^2|g_\ell|^{2m}\le(\max_\ell|g_\ell|^m)^2\|v\|_{2,h}^2$. Since the finite set of modes has an index attaining this maximum and its basis vector is nonzero, equality is attained there; [F4] therefore gives $\|T^m\|=\max_\ell|g_\ell|^m$. The bounds and growing modes in steps 1.1 and 1.2 now give the claimed contraction and instability statements, including the $N=2$ aliasing cases. [F1, F2, F3, F4, F5, step 1.1, step 1.2] ∎

## Statement

Fix $a\in\mathbb R\setminus\{0\}$. Let $u:\mathbb R^2\to\mathbb R$ be a $C^6$ solution of $u_t+a u_x=0$ that is periodic in $x$ with period $P>0$, so $u(x+P,t)=u(x,t)$, and whose derivatives through order six are bounded. Let $h,k\to0$ with $0<c_-\le k/h\le c_+<\infty$, and put $\nu=|a|k/h$. For a stencil $S$, define its local residual by
$$ \tau_S(x,t)=\frac{u(x,t+k)-S(u(\cdot,t))(x)}{k}. $$
Then, for the sign-selected stencils of [[def-periodic-one-way-advection-schemes]], the upwind, downwind, centered, and Lax--Friedrichs residuals are $O(h)$ uniformly in $(x,t)$, while the Lax--Wendroff residual is $O(h^2)$. Here a remainder $R=O(\eta(h,k))$ uniformly means $|R(x,t;h,k)|\le C\eta(h,k)$ for all $x,t$ and sufficiently small $h,k$, with $C$ independent of $x,t,h,k$ under the stated ratio bounds. These are smooth-solution consistency statements and imply no convergence result at discontinuities.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The stated smooth solution, fixed nonzero speed $a$, and two-sided mesh ratio $c_-\le k/h\le c_+$.

[F1] The five periodic stencils use the stated sign convention for $a>0$ and are reflected by $j\mapsto-j$ for $a<0$, with $\nu=|a|k/h$ ([[def-periodic-one-way-advection-schemes]]).

[F2] If derivatives through order $m+1$ are bounded on the segment, the order-$m$ Taylor polynomial has a remainder bounded by the derivative bound times the corresponding power divided by $(m+1)!$ ([[cor-taylor-remainder-bound]]).

[F3] For a function on an open subset of $\mathbb R^2$, $C^6$ means that every iterated partial derivative of total order at most six exists and is continuous ([[def-ck-and-multi-index-notation-in-several-variables]]).

[F4] For a $C^k$ function, iterated partial derivatives of order $k$ are unchanged by permuting the coordinate differentiations ([[thm-symmetry-of-higher-mixed-partials]]).

## Proof

1.1 If $a<0$, set $A=-a>0$ and $\widetilde u(x,t)=u(-x,t)$. For fixed $x$, its time difference quotient is that of $u$ at $(-x,t)$, so $\widetilde u_t(x,t)=u_t(-x,t)$. In its spatial difference quotient, substitute $s=-h$ to get $\widetilde u_x(x,t)=-u_x(-x,t)$. Repeating these coordinate calculations gives $\partial_x^p\partial_t^q\widetilde u(x,t)=(-1)^p(\partial_x^p\partial_t^q u)(-x,t)$, so the period and derivative bounds are preserved. The PDE gives $\widetilde u_t+A\widetilde u_x=u_t(-x,t)-A u_x(-x,t)=0$. The definition's reflection $j\mapsto-j$ identifies each negative-speed stencil residual with the corresponding positive-speed residual of $\widetilde u$ at the reflected point. If $a>0$, take $A=a$ and $\widetilde u=u$. It is therefore enough to derive the estimates for positive speed $A$. [given, F1, F3, construct, algebra]

2.1 For this positive-speed solution, differentiating $\widetilde u_t=-A\widetilde u_x$ in $t$ and $x$, then using [F4] to commute the order-two mixed partials, gives $\widetilde u_{tt}=-A\widetilde u_{xt}=-A\widetilde u_{tx}=A^2\widetilde u_{xx}$. Differentiating this identity in $t$ and the PDE twice in $x$, then using [F4] to commute the order-three partials, gives $\widetilde u_{ttt}=A^2\widetilde u_{xxt}=A^2\widetilde u_{txx}=-A^3\widetilde u_{xxx}$. By [F3] these derivatives exist, and the bounded derivatives in the hypotheses make the Taylor remainders uniform. Taylor's formula from [F2] yields $$ \frac{\widetilde u(x,t+k)-\widetilde u(x,t)}{k}=\widetilde u_t+\frac{k}{2}\widetilde u_{tt}+\frac{k^2}{6}\widetilde u_{ttt}+O(k^3), $$ $$ \frac{\widetilde u(x+h,t)-\widetilde u(x-h,t)}{2h}=\widetilde u_x+\frac{h^2}{6}\widetilde u_{xxx}+O(h^4),\qquad \frac{\widetilde u(x+h,t)-2\widetilde u(x,t)+\widetilde u(x-h,t)}{h^2}=\widetilde u_{xx}+\frac{h^2}{12}\widetilde u_{xxxx}+O(h^4). $$ The one-sided expansions are $(\widetilde u(x,t)-\widetilde u(x-h,t))/h=\widetilde u_x-\frac h2\widetilde u_{xx}+O(h^2)$ and $(\widetilde u(x+h,t)-\widetilde u(x,t))/h=\widetilde u_x+\frac h2\widetilde u_{xx}+O(h^2)$. [given, F2, F3, F4, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 Substituting the step 2.1 expansions into [F1] with speed $A=|a|$ and using $\widetilde u_t+A\widetilde u_x=0$ gives $$ \tau_{\rm up}=\frac{k}{2}\widetilde u_{tt}-\frac{Ah}{2}\widetilde u_{xx}+O(k^2+h^2),\quad \tau_{\rm down}=\frac{k}{2}\widetilde u_{tt}+\frac{Ah}{2}\widetilde u_{xx}+O(k^2+h^2),\quad \tau_{\rm centered}=\frac{k}{2}\widetilde u_{tt}+O(k^2+h^2). $$ For Lax--Friedrichs the symmetric average contributes $-h^2\widetilde u_{xx}/(2k)$ to the residual, so $\tau_{\rm LF}=\frac{k}{2}\widetilde u_{tt}-\frac{h^2}{2k}\widetilde u_{xx}+O(k^2+h^2+h^4/k)$. For Lax--Wendroff the $k\widetilde u_{tt}/2$ term cancels the second-difference term by $\widetilde u_{tt}=A^2\widetilde u_{xx}$, leaving $\tau_{\rm LW}=\frac{k^2}{6}\widetilde u_{ttt}+\frac{Ah^2}{6}\widetilde u_{xxx}+O(k^3+h^4+kh^2)$. Reflection in step 1.1 transfers these residual bounds to the negative-speed branch. [F1, step 1.1, step 2.1, algebra]

4.1 The mesh ratio bounds imply $k=O(h)$ and $h^2/k=O(h)$. Thus the first four residuals are uniformly $O(h)$, and every displayed Lax--Wendroff term is $O(h^2)$ or smaller. By step 1.1 the same estimates hold for either velocity sign. The conclusion concerns only the sampled smooth solution in the stated periodic setting. [given, step 1.1, step 3.1, algebra] ∎

This page develops two related but distinct structured-population models. The age model follows unit-speed age characteristics with mortality and a renewal birth boundary. It supplies the characteristic/Volterra solution, the absorbing finite-age version, positive birth quadrature, and an explicit upwind finite-volume scheme. Under the transport-plus-loss CFL, the scheme preserves nonnegativity and satisfies a discrete mass bound. Compatible smooth data give a first-order cell-mass and reconstructed-density estimate when the true birth quadrature defect is controlled. BV data need no initial boundary compatibility; the separate compactness argument gives (L^1) convergence without a Taylor rate.

The cutoff analysis keeps survival, outflow, and the initial-age tail visible as a separate error. The cohort method advances ages exactly and approximates survival and births; its consistency result is in bounded-Lipschitz measure norm, not (L^1) for atomic measures. A narrow maturation profile approaches a delayed birth term under stated Lipschitz bounds, while a finite-width kernel is not an exact delay. Capped adaptive indicators do not certify true quadrature error.

The size model uses a fixed interval, strictly positive growth, an absorbing upper boundary, parent removal, and a measurable nonlocal daughter kernel. Its variable-width finite-volume update uses positive daughter coefficients and gives exact discrete number and center-weighted-size balances. The first moment is conserved by division only when daughter-size production cancels parent removal; an arbitrary kernel need not satisfy that identity. Moving boundaries, zero growth, and discontinuous coefficients are outside this model.

This page defines five scalar advection stencils on periodic or infinite uniform grids and the upwind inflow row on a finite interval. It proves smooth consistency orders, exact periodic Fourier power bounds, and the necessity of a nearest-neighbor domain-of-dependence CFL condition. A fixed-period centered-advection family is smooth-consistent but has no uniform finite-time power bound even with $ak/h=1/2$. For the centered leapfrog wave recurrence, the page proves the discrete Dirichlet summation identity, a conserved coercive energy for $0<ck/h<1$, and periodic amplification estimates with explicit treatment of the mean and repeated Nyquist modes; its start data are displacement and discrete initial velocity. Periodic Fourier bounds do not establish finite-boundary stability; smooth consistency does not imply convergence at discontinuities.
